punctuated:
夫豈面謀之已邪？夫知之既深，任之有不重哉？蓋人君為天宗子，則所以奉天者宜無不盡也。以此宅俊而敬事之，與之共天位也，精白一心，昭其篤棐之忱焉；與之治天職也，夙夜匪懈，勵其庶明之翼焉。蓋天之所畀於君者，咸資宅俊以代其終矣。人君作民元后，則所以子民者亦宜無不周也。以此宅俊而長伯之，立之以厚民生也，而容保無疆，擴吾惠鮮之澤焉；立之以正民德也，而教思無窮，弘吾怙冒之仁焉。蓋民之所望於君者，咸藉宅俊以成其能矣。夫惟上帝之事，則職業修，而所以膺純佑之眷者在此也；夫惟長伯之立，則體統正，而所以底允懷之休者在此也。此文武克知灼見之效，而知恤之實，不亦從可徵哉？
嗟夫！萬化之原涵於一心，而帝王之所以參賛天地、左右斯民者，咸此心為之運也。周之文武，敬止建中，心學邃矣。故其任賢圖治，必究觀其心，而不敢以輕用；而當時為之臣者，亦皆殫心靖恭以事其上。此所以志同道
translation_en:
Could this have been merely a matter of consulting them face to face? Once their understanding of these men was profound, how could the responsibilities entrusted to them be anything but weighty? The ruler is Heaven’s principal heir, and so he should leave nothing undone in serving Heaven. On this basis he places worthy men in office and reverently serves Heaven. Sharing Heaven’s positions with them, he makes his heart pure and spotless, displaying his sincerity in offering steadfast assistance to Heaven; administering Heaven’s duties with them, he remains tireless day and night, encouraging the aid of men possessed of manifold understanding. Thus, all that Heaven entrusts to the ruler depends upon placing worthy men in office to carry it through on his behalf. The ruler is the people’s sovereign, and so his care for them as his children should likewise extend everywhere. On this basis he places worthy men in office and makes them leaders. He establishes them to enrich the people’s livelihood: by embracing and protecting the people without limit, they extend his beneficence in caring for those in distress. He establishes them to rectify the people’s virtue: through unending concern for instruction, they enlarge his benevolence in sheltering and protecting the people. Thus, everything the people expect of their ruler depends upon placing worthy men in office to bring his capacities to fulfillment. Through service to the Lord on High, official duties are properly discharged; herein lies the means of receiving the favor of Heaven’s abundant protection. Through the establishment of leaders, the proper order of authority is secured; herein lies the means of attaining the blessing of the people’s sincere attachment. Such were the effects of Kings Wen and Wu’s thorough knowledge and clear discernment. Can we not also verify from these the substance of their understanding and solicitude?
Alas! The source of all transformation is contained within a single heart. It is this heart that directs everything by which emperors and kings assist Heaven and Earth and guide and aid the people. Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou rested in reverence and established the mean: profound indeed was their learning of the heart. Thus, when appointing worthy men and seeking good government, they invariably examined those men’s hearts thoroughly and dared not employ them lightly. Those who served as their ministers at that time likewise devoted their whole hearts to serving their sovereign with quiet reverence. This was why their purposes were the same and their Way…

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: “You elucidate the heart that cherishes its ruler: its spontaneous feeling is almost palpable. Surely you are one of today’s worthy men!”

A great minister who promotes worthy men possesses the loyalty that seeks to serve his ruler; profound indeed are the hopes he places in them. Loyalty and love for their ruler are aspirations shared by all worthy men. It depends only on whether the ruler can employ them. How could any fail to render service? This is an ode in which Duke Kang of Shao admonishes King Cheng; at this point, he urges him to employ worthy men. Its meaning seems to be: Now, as for the phoenixes in flight…

其上之而戾于天者性也乃復翽翽其羽集于

夫物固有性士固有志苟遂其志安使而弗効

punctuated: 其上之而戾于天者，性也。乃復翽翽其羽，集于所止者，何哉？蓋其飛戾天者，性適于飛也；其集所止者，性適于止也。苟適其性，則無往不之矣。夫物固有性，士固有志。苟遂其志，安使而弗効乎？載觀今日之天下，吾王之吉士，何藹藹其衆也！蓋天之所生，固將以足一時之用；而志之所存，又欲以覲天子之光。其所以未効于王者，以吾王未之使耳。誠能以賢之不可遺也，而用之不厭其多；以才之不可枉也，而使之各當其能，吾見大而有成德之士也，王以德使，則何德而不爲媚乎？爲之先後焉，爲之左右焉。雖聖脩無待于外求，而區區補袞之忠，蓋有弗能自已者矣。小而有達材之士也，王以材使，則何材而不爲媚乎？爲之明其則焉，爲之理其綱焉。雖神化不資乎小補，而拳拳賛治之圖，蓋有弗能竟忘者矣。感遭逢之盛也，無所不順，而順于道，非道不敢陳，固平生之所學者耳。思知遇之難也，無所不愛，而愛以德，一德之相孚，固素心之自許
translation_en:
…that it rises and reaches heaven is its nature. Why, then, does it again rustle its wings and alight in its resting place? When it flies to heaven, its nature finds satisfaction in flight; when it alights in its resting place, its nature finds satisfaction in repose. If its nature is satisfied, there is nowhere it will not go. Just as creatures have their natures, so gentlemen have their aspirations. If their aspirations are fulfilled, in what service could they fail to give their utmost?

Consider now the realm today: how abundant are our king’s worthy gentlemen! Heaven has brought them forth precisely to meet the needs of their age, and their own aspirations lead them to seek an audience in the radiance of the Son of Heaven. The reason they have not yet rendered service to the king is simply that our king has not employed them. If he truly recognizes that worthy men must not be passed over, employing them without finding their numbers excessive, and that talents must not be misapplied, assigning each man duties suited to his abilities, then I foresee the following.

At the higher level are gentlemen of perfected virtue. If the king employs them according to their virtue, what virtue will they not bring to bear in showing him their devotion? They will serve before and behind him, to his left and right. Although his sagely self-cultivation requires no assistance from outside, their humble loyalty in mending the royal robe—that is, remedying the ruler’s shortcomings—will surely be impossible to restrain. At the lesser level are gentlemen of accomplished ability. If the king employs them according to their talents, what talent will they not bring to bear in showing him their devotion? They will clarify his standards and put the guiding principles of his government in order. Although his wondrous transforming influence does not depend on minor assistance, they will surely never be able to put aside their earnest intention to aid his rule.

Moved by the greatness of their good fortune in finding such a ruler, they will be obedient in all things, yet their obedience will accord with the Way. They will not dare present anything contrary to the Way: this is simply what they have learned throughout their lives. Reflecting on how difficult it is to find a ruler who recognizes and appreciates them, they will show love in all things, yet love him through virtue. Mutual trust grounded in a shared virtue is precisely what they have always inwardly pledged themselves to…

者耳。觀此，則士之慕君也不爲不切，而君之得士也亦不爲無益焉。成王者，寧能弗加之意邪？且成王，有周之令主也，然又撫成業而履盛運，夫復何虞？康公從游卷阿而諭戒不已者，何也？蓋保治獲福，莫要於用賢；而太平之世，雖有賢者，無以自見，故汲汲焉欲其亟用之耳，亦先事豫圖之意也。毋其時鳳凰見祥，恐將驕主心而忽治道，遂因以爲諭乎？老成愛君之意，誠無窮哉！

我受命溥將，自天降康，豐年穰穰。

translation_en:
…that is all. From this we see that the devotion of worthy men to their ruler is indeed earnest, and that a ruler’s acquisition of such men is certainly beneficial. Could King Cheng fail to give this his attention? Moreover, King Cheng was an excellent ruler of the Zhou. He inherited an established enterprise and enjoyed a flourishing age: what further cause had he for concern? Why, then, did Duke Kang, accompanying him on an excursion to Juan’e, continue to admonish him without cease? Because nothing is more essential to preserving good government and securing blessings than employing the worthy. Yet in an age of peace, even worthy men have no means of making themselves known. Thus the duke urgently wished the king to employ them without delay; this too expressed his intention to plan ahead before difficulties arose. Could it be that, when the phoenix appeared as an auspicious sign, he feared that it would make the ruler proud and neglectful of the way of good government, and therefore used the occasion to admonish him? [?] Truly inexhaustible is the devotion of a seasoned elder to his ruler!

“We have received a vast and great mandate; from Heaven descends well-being, with bountiful harvests in abundance.”
By Cheng Zhongyin 成鍾音.

Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: “The style of the ‘Hymns of Shang’ is concise and plain. This composition captures it.”

Associate Examiner Jiang, Instructor, comments: “In treating this topic, essays generally become confused and wordy when addressing the relationship between Heaven and humanity. None equals this piece in expressing its meaning fully with few words.”

Associate Examiner Luo, metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: “The other compositions are mostly wordy, jumbled, and forced in their connections. This piece alone is precise in wording and thought. It is selected to promote refined writing.”

Examiner Yuan, Expositor, comments: “Concise and clear.”

The worthy king describes the abundance of Heaven’s favor and then its further renewal, revealing how far the blessings bestowed of old extend. By gathering the people’s hearts to participate in sacrifice, Shang had already received Heaven’s abundant favor. Yet Heaven further bestowed years of plenty: how great, then, was its renewal of the mandate through blessings! Here we may discern what Tang bequeathed.

In former times, the people of Shang sang the hymn “Illustrious Ancestor” to sacrifice to Tang. At this point they say: “The blessings of a state must have their beginnings laid beforehand. Heaven’s blessing upon Tang’s virtue was supreme, and remains unchanged even now. Should we not also seek its evidence in the people’s hearts?”

Now, when the king approaches the temple and the many lords all come, the filial devotion with which this one man continues to serve his departed ancestor wins the delight of the myriad states. When the grand offering begins and all within the realm of common carriage tracks arrive, the sincerity with which the succeeding king honors his ancestor accords with the willing submission of the people’s hearts. Heaven is difficult to rely upon; the evidence of its favor lies in human beings. Now, at the time of reverent worship, all under Heaven follow one another to attend. Thus the king receives Heaven’s blessings, and the hundred favors converge upon him. How far-reaching is the mandate he receives!

Heaven has no partial affections; the workings of its favor depend upon those below. Now, as the participants hasten to their duties, all under Heaven turn toward the king. Thus he receives Heaven’s favor, and the hundred blessings gather upon him. How great is the mandate he receives!

Yet once the mandate has become so far-reaching, I begin to fear that I cannot worthily uphold its divine charge; still, Heaven’s benevolent love knows no end. Yin and yang are harmonious, and the year brings plenty, bestowing upon me the joy of an abundant harvest. Once the mandate has become so great, I begin to fear that I am unworthy to receive such favor; still, Heaven’s generous gifts do not cease. Rain and sunshine come in their proper seasons, and the year yields abundance, comforting me with the blessing of crops duly ripened. 為嘉栗旨酒以繼孝於祖考者，何不備也！有稻有秬，而嘉種浩穰，凡吾致潔粢豐盛以陳信於鬼神者，何不周也！是其自天申之，維日不足如此，則今之辟公相而熈事成者，固皆天命之匪懈，而烈祖祈天之永，不尤可繹思也哉？記禮者之言曰：「肆直而慈愛者宜歌商。」蓋商道尚質，其心懇至，而其言簡明。是故登歌之頌，稱述祖德，無溢美矯飾之詞；而事神之頃，無言無爭，肅敬齊一，肆直慈愛之意藹然可挹。故今讀烈祖之頌，尚可想見而興起也。雖然，以湯為祖而受命，以武丁為孫而中興，重光之德昭格天人，天之佑商而綿其曆也，固宜。

translation_en:
…what could be lacking among the fine grain [?] and excellent wine we prepare to continue our filial service to our ancestors? There are rice and black millet, and fine crops grow in abundance. What could be wanting among the pure sacrificial grain and plentiful offerings we present to demonstrate our sincerity to the spirits? Heaven thus bestows its gifts repeatedly, as though the days were insufficient. Hence the lords who now assist at the sacrifice and bring its splendid rites to completion all exemplify the unceasing operation of Heaven’s mandate. Should we not ponder still more deeply how the illustrious ancestor prayed to Heaven for its enduring favor?

The compiler of the Record of Rites said: “Those who are frank and upright, compassionate and loving, should sing the hymns of Shang.” The way of Shang prized simplicity: its sentiments were deeply sincere, and its words concise and clear. Thus the hymns sung in the hall recount ancestral virtue without exaggerated praise or artificial embellishment. During service to the spirits, there was neither speaking nor contention; all were solemn, reverent, and united. Their frankness, uprightness, compassion, and love were so abundant that one could almost draw them forth. Thus, even today, reading the hymn “Illustrious Ancestor,” we can still envision these qualities and be inspired by them. Yet with Tang as the ancestor who received the mandate, and Wu Ding as the descendant who restored the dynasty, the virtue of their successive brilliance reached Heaven and humanity alike. It was surely fitting that Heaven should protect Shang and prolong its allotted span.

text:
考試官右諭德王批得謹嚴體
春秋予伯者之兵以其舉之有名而用之有制
也蓋有名則非妄動矣有制則非黷武矣伯者
之兵有是哉春秋安得而不予且宋人背北杏
之盟齊連三國之師以伐之亦春秋之常事耳
然而書伐宋又稱人者予之也夫其予之者何
蓋書伐宋者予其爲有名之師也自王室既微
桓公欲以盟會而申尊周之義而宋首背之是
兵之招也故聯璧壓境非以耀武問不信也移
檄數罪非以易齊討無君也夫東遷以来諸侯
邪僻固有非義伺人者矣而伐宋之役則興戎
者不爲幸禍而納侮者不爲無妄此所謂有名
之師事靡不成者也卒之言直氣壯而宋珹見
取焉謂非協人心而合天理之驗乎春秋予之
者以此其稱人者予其爲有制之兵也蓋寓兵
于民管仲将以富强而建圖伯之勲而兵數用
焉是民之厲也故邦有大夫而未嘗有推轂之
遣懼傷財也邦有大衆而未嘗有傾國之行懼

Examiner Wang, Right Mentor, comments: “Achieves a disciplined and rigorous style.”

The Spring and Autumn Annals approves the military undertakings of hegemons because they are launched for a legitimate cause and conducted with restraint. A legitimate cause precludes reckless action; restraint precludes wanton warfare. When a hegemon’s military undertakings possess these qualities, how could the Spring and Autumn Annals withhold its approval? The men of Song violated the covenant of Beixing, and Qi joined the armies of three states to attack them: this was simply an ordinary occurrence in the Spring and Autumn Annals. Yet its recording of the attack on Song, and its designation of the participants as “men,” express approval. Why does it approve?

In recording the attack on Song, it approves an army acting for a legitimate cause. After the royal house had declined, Duke Huan sought through covenants and assemblies to uphold the duty of honoring Zhou. Song was the first to break faith, thereby inviting military action. Thus the allied forces pressed upon its borders not to display martial might, but to demand an accounting for its breach of faith. They circulated proclamations enumerating its offenses not to alter Qi [?], but to punish its disregard for its sovereign. Since the eastward relocation of the Zhou court, there had certainly been depraved feudal lords who unjustly watched for opportunities to prey upon others. In the campaign against Song, however, those who initiated hostilities were not exploiting another’s misfortune, while those who brought attack upon themselves were not suffering an undeserved calamity. This is what is meant by an army with a legitimate cause, whose undertakings invariably succeed. In the end, their case was just and their spirit resolute, and a city of Song [?] was captured. Was this not proof that they accorded with human hearts and conformed to Heaven’s principle? This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals approves them.

In calling them “men,” it approves their army’s restraint. Military service was embedded in the populace, and Guan Zhong intended to establish the achievement of hegemony through wealth and strength. Yet frequent military operations would afflict the people. Thus, although the state had grand masters, none was dispatched with the ceremonial pushing of a commander’s carriage, for fear of draining its resources. 伯功興聖王之綱紀猶得不絶如綫者齊桓故
也而聖王之綱紀漸以澌滅者亦齊桓故也何
===
也宋先王之後也雖其罪可討夫齊安得而擅
伐之三國稱人雖志同欲也齊亦安得而擅用
之此伯道之盛王道之衰所由始也故曰五伯
者三王之罪人也
夏公會齊侯于夾谷公至自夾谷〔定公十年〕
同考試官知縣毛　批〔夾谷之會此聖人俄頃之化是作善於模寫其知聖人之精者乎〕
趙以文
punctuated:
勞力也。夫西周之後，諸侯放恣，固有非法動衆者矣。而伐宋之役，則將卑而從軍之費寡，師少而賦民之法薄，此所謂有制之兵，所向無敵者也。卒之南摧西抑，而天下莫爭焉，謂非既富國而又强兵之効乎？春秋予之者以此。用是而觀，兵貴以義，義則有名；亦貴以仁，仁則有制。齊之師進于是矣，其伯天下也宜哉！抑自王迹熄而伯功興，聖王之綱紀猶得不絕如綫者，齊桓故也；而聖王之綱紀漸以澌滅者，亦齊桓故也。何也？宋，先王之後也。雖其罪可討，夫齊安得而擅伐之？三國稱人，雖志同欲也，齊亦安得而擅用之？此伯道之盛、王道之衰所由始也。故曰：「五伯者，三王之罪人也。」
夏，公會齊侯于夾谷。公至自夾谷。定公十年。
趙以文
同考試官知縣毛批：「夾谷之會，此聖人俄頃之化。是作善於模寫，其知聖人之精者乎！」
translation_en:
…to avoid exhausting the people's strength. After the Western Zhou, the regional lords became unrestrained, and there were certainly those who mobilized their people unlawfully. Yet in the campaign against Song, the commander's rank was low and the expenses of military service were modest; the army was small and the levies imposed upon the people were light. This was what is called a regulated army, invincible wherever it advances. In the end, it crushed opposition in the south and checked it in the west, and none under Heaven could contend with it. Was this not proof of success in both enriching the state and strengthening its army? This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals approves of it. Viewed in this light, military action must prize righteousness: righteousness gives it a legitimate cause. It must also prize benevolence: benevolence keeps it within proper bounds. Qi's army attained this standard. How fitting that its ruler became hegemon over all under Heaven!
Yet after the legacy of the kings faded and the achievements of the hegemons arose, it was because of Duke Huan of Qi that the institutions and ordering principles of the sage kings survived, tenuous as a thread. It was also because of Duke Huan of Qi that those institutions and principles gradually dissolved. Why? Song was the state of the former kings' descendants. Although its offenses deserved punishment, how could Qi presume to attack it on its own authority? Although the three states, whose participants are designated as “men,” shared a common purpose, how could Qi presume to employ them on its own authority? Here began the ascendancy of the hegemonic way and the decline of the kingly way. Thus it is said: “The Five Hegemons were offenders against the Three Kings.”
“In summer, the duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu. The duke returned from Jiagu.” Tenth year of Duke Ding.
Zhao Yiwen
Comment by Associate Examiner Mao, Magistrate: “The meeting at Jiagu exemplifies the sage's power to transform a situation in an instant. This composition portrays it skillfully. Surely its author understands the subtle workings of the sage!”

考試官侍講袁批善說聖人神化
考試官右諭德王批有斷制
聖人相禮而化强亦惟順乎理而已夫天下莫
大于理而强眾不與焉此夾谷之會齊之所以
謝夫魯歟且夫景公惑犁彌之謀而會定公于
夾谷也夫固以爲可得志也定公信孔子之言
而具司馬以從也夫亦以爲備患圖也迨夫壇
坫之位甫就而鼓譟之聲遽起會同之禮未舉
而兵甲之刼已臨當是時也定公蓋危若懸綴
===
而患在須臾矣孔子乃不爲應敵之兵而徒事
歷階之諍彼司馬之從者何爲者邪意以爲以
兵偪好彼齊已蹈夫夷狄之俗矣尤而效之非
所以明有義也以禮爲國我魯蓋世守先王之
法矣見難而廢非所以昭君德也迨乎謀夏亂
華之言出而强梁者遂服愆義失禮之讓至而

聖人相禮而化强，亦惟順乎理而已。夫天下莫大于理，而强眾不與焉。此夾谷之會，齊之所以謝夫魯歟？且夫景公惑犁彌之謀而會定公于夾谷也，夫固以爲可得志也；定公信孔子之言而具司馬以從也，夫亦以爲備患圖也。迨夫壇坫之位甫就，而鼓譟之聲遽起；會同之禮未舉，而兵甲之刼已臨。當是時也，定公蓋危若懸綴，而患在須臾矣。孔子乃不爲應敵之兵，而徒事歷階之諍，彼司馬之從者何爲者邪？意以爲以兵偪好，彼齊已蹈夫夷狄之俗矣；尤而效之，非所以明有義也。以禮爲國，我魯蓋世守先王之法矣；見難而廢，非所以昭君德也。迨乎謀夏亂華之言出，而强梁者遂服；愆義失禮之讓至，而狙詐者自消。其君即以狄道自任，而推魯于古人之列；其臣即欲謝過以質，而歸魯以見侵之田。蓋不惟饗禮用成，而揖讓之體不失，且能使
translation_en:
Examiner Yuan, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “It explains well the sage’s wondrous transforming influence.”
Examiner Wang, Right Admonisher, comments: “It shows decisive judgment.”
The sage assisted in conducting the rites and thereby transformed the violent; he did so simply by following moral principle. Nothing under Heaven is greater than principle; force and superior numbers cannot compare with it. Was this not why Qi apologized to Lu at the meeting at Jiagu?
Duke Jing, misled by Li Mi’s scheme, met Duke Ding at Jiagu, firmly believing that he could achieve his purpose. Duke Ding, trusting Confucius’s advice, arranged for a Minister of War to accompany him, likewise considering this a precaution against trouble. Yet scarcely had they taken their places at the ceremonial platform when drumming and shouting suddenly arose. Before the rites of the interstate meeting had begun, armed coercion was already upon them. At that moment Duke Ding’s position was as precarious as something hanging by a thread, and disaster was imminent.
Confucius, however, made no military response to the enemy, but merely mounted the steps to remonstrate. What, then, was the purpose of having the Minister of War accompany them? His reasoning was this: by using armed force to constrain a friendly state, Qi had already fallen into the customs of the Yi and Di peoples. To condemn this conduct and then imitate it would do nothing to demonstrate righteousness. In governing through ritual, our state of Lu had upheld the laws of the former kings for generations. To abandon them when confronted with danger would do nothing to manifest its ruler’s virtue.
Once Confucius spoke of plotting against the Xia and disrupting the Hua—the civilized states—the violent submitted. Once he rebuked their offenses against righteousness and ritual, the schemers’ deceit dissolved of itself. Their ruler acknowledged that his own conduct followed the ways of the Di, while placing Lu among the ranks of the ancients. Their minister then sought to give tangible substance to the apology by returning to Lu the lands that had been seized from it. Thus not only were the ceremonial courtesies brought to fulfillment, with the forms of bowing and yielding preserved, but he was also able to bring about…

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
返國有光而君子之躬無恙此可與恃强用衆
者同日而語邪若使齊以兵刦而我亦以兵應
則兩國合好而顧以亂終即不可示之天下矣
豈有魯君之在會而可令其如此也魯有忿心
則齊且將得志奉君以出而或令見辱即不可
告之宗廟矣豈有孔子之爲相而肯使至于此
極也故書曰公會曰蓋美其有備也曰公至蓋紀
其不辱也由是觀之則一言之重勇于三軍率
理之爲勝一于率衆其斯以爲聖乎是會也亦可
===
以見聖人與人爲善之心焉蓋春秋重補過不
遠而復景公有之納約自牖晏子亦允蹈焉要
其初則皆孔子歷階之諍有以感之也於乎歷
階不盡既先以禮檢其躬矣壇上之觀者奈何
不服余獨恠以晏子爲相而令犁彌得行其說
誠所謂不知仲尼者邪
禮記
仁者義之本也順之體也得之者尊
潘允端

===
以見聖人與人爲善之心焉蓋春秋重補過不
遠而復景公有之納約自牖晏子亦允蹈焉要
其初則背孔子歷階之諍有以感之也於乎歷

不服余獨惜以晏子爲相而令犂彌得行其說
誠所謂不知仲尼者邪
禮記
仁者天下之表也義者天下之制也仁者右也
punctuated:
返國有光，而君子之躬無恙，此可與恃强用衆者同日而語邪？若使齊以兵刦，而我亦以兵應，則兩國合好而顧以亂終，即不可示之天下矣。豈有魯君之在會，而可令其如此也？魯有忿心，則齊且將得志；奉君以出，而或令見辱，即不可告之宗廟矣。豈有孔子之爲相，而肯使至于此極也？故書曰「公會」曰，蓋美其有備也；曰「公至」，蓋紀其不辱也。由是觀之，則一言之重，勇于三軍；率理之爲勝，一于率衆，其斯以爲聖乎？是會也，亦可以見聖人與人爲善之心焉。蓋春秋重補過，不遠而復，景公有之；納約自牖，晏子亦允蹈焉。要其初，則皆孔子歷階之諍有以感之也。於乎！歷階不盡，既先以禮檢其躬矣，壇上之觀者奈何不服？余獨恠以晏子爲相，而令犁彌得行其說，誠所謂不知仲尼者邪？

禮記
仁者，義之本也，順之體也，得之者尊。
潘允端
translation_en:
…return to his state with honor, while the noble ruler himself remained unharmed. Can this be spoken of in the same breath as relying on force and deploying large numbers? Had Qi used troops to coerce us, and had we likewise responded with troops, the two states would have come together in friendship only to end in disorder: such an outcome could not have been displayed before the world. With the lord of Lu attending the meeting, how could matters have been allowed to come to this? If Lu acted out of anger, Qi would thereby achieve its purpose. To escort one’s ruler abroad and perhaps allow him to suffer humiliation would make it impossible to report the affair to the ancestral temple. With Confucius serving as ceremonial assistant, how could he have been willing to let matters reach such an extremity? Thus the record says, “The duke met”—praising his preparedness [the additional 曰 in the transcription is doubtful]; it says, “The duke arrived”—recording that he suffered no humiliation. Viewed in this light, the weight of a single utterance exceeds the valor of the Three Armies; following principle surpasses leading a multitude [?]. Is this what makes him a sage?

This meeting also reveals the sage’s desire to help others do good. The Spring and Autumn Annals values the correction of faults: Duke Jing exemplified “returning before going far.” Yanzi, too, truly practiced “presenting simple offerings through the window.” Ultimately, what first moved them both was Confucius’s remonstrance as he ascended the steps. Ah! By ascending without reaching the final step, he had already first disciplined his own conduct through ritual propriety. How could those watching on the platform fail to submit? I only marvel that, with Yanzi serving as chief minister, Li Mi was allowed to put his proposal into practice. Was Yanzi truly, as the saying goes, one who did not understand Zhongni?

Book of Rites
“Benevolence is the root of righteousness and the embodiment of accord; those who attain it are honored.”
Pan Yunduan

Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: “There was no shortage of candidates writing on this topic, but their treatment was bogged down [?]. As for concision of wording combined with completeness of meaning, none equals this essay. I select it for inclusion.”

Examiner Yuan, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Clear and clean.”

Examiner Wang, Right Admonisher, comments: “The passages explaining the fundamental substance are all exceptionally refined.”

The recorder discusses the greatness of fully realizing the Way of benevolence and the consequent fitness to undertake leadership over others. For only the benevolent ought to occupy high positions. When one has attained it without any particular good [?], benevolence becomes complete within oneself. Is it not fitting, then, to occupy an exalted position? The intention of the recorder of the “Evolution of Rites” seems to be that, as a Way, benevolence, when gathered together, serves to order the dispositions of all under Heaven; embodied in oneself, it suffices to bear the weight of all under Heaven. Is this benevolence, then, not what the sage kings established as preeminent?

Now benevolence unites what is alike, while righteousness distinguishes what differs. Their functions seem to stand apart. Yet benevolence is the origin of virtue, and righteousness takes its root therein. Adapting and judging so as to respond fully to change is entirely the ordering work of this mind; weighing and measuring so as to regulate affairs is wholly the flowing operation of our principle of life. Thus thoughts of utmost sincerity and compassionate concern are thoroughly integrated into the work of shaping, deciding, and regulating, and the Way of righteousness thereby becomes manifest. Is benevolence not what makes this righteousness benevolent?

Benevolence perfects oneself, while accord brings other beings to fulfillment. Their outward workings seem to diverge. Yet benevolence is foremost among forms of goodness, and accord derives its substance from it. That the Way wins trust within family and state is rooted in the fullness and all-embracing reach of loving care; that transforming influence shines far and near originates in the overflowing of utmost kindness. Thus the wondrous mutual flow of joy and delight animates the blessings of harmonious vital energies and flourishing life, and the workings of accord thereby find free expression. title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以體此順邪夫其合義順而成仁則有以統天
下之善矣人而有得之者庸歉於居尊之任乎
夫仁爲尊爵所以立萬夫之望而義以行之則
處無不宜而天下各得其所以是而履帝位寧
復有所疚哉仁爲廣居所以啓人心之歸而順
以出之則施無不當而天下各適其情以是而
臨大君寧不允所稱哉蓋德之所在既有以涵
天地之大則位之所在自足以居聖人之寶矣
體仁以長人其道固如此是則所該者博體之
===
會其全也所任者尊用之達其妙也此仁道之
所以爲大而先王修禮以治情舍仁其何本哉
抑聞之經禮三百曲禮三千無一事而非仁此
窮本之論也夫先王宰制羣動役使萬物固由
於大禮之節然非吾心之仁彌綸貫徹於其間
禮亦烏能以自行哉是知爲國以禮爲禮以仁

體仁以長人其道固如此是則所該者博體之
===
會其全也所任者尊用之達其妙也此仁道之
所以爲大而先王修禮以治情舍仁其何本哉
抑聞之經禮三百曲禮三千無一事而非仁此

punctuated:
以體此順邪？夫其合義順而成仁，則有以統天下之善矣。人而有得之者，庸歉於居尊之任乎？夫仁爲尊爵，所以立萬夫之望，而義以行之，則處無不宜，而天下各得其所，以是而履帝位，寧復有所疚哉？仁爲廣居，所以啓人心之歸，而順以出之，則施無不當，而天下各適其情，以是而臨大君，寧不允所稱哉？蓋德之所在，既有以涵天地之大，則位之所在，自足以居聖人之寶矣。體仁以長人，其道固如此。是則所該者博，體之會其全也；所任者尊，用之達其妙也。此仁道之所以爲大，而先王修禮以治情，舍仁其何本哉？

抑聞之，經禮三百，曲禮三千，無一事而非仁，此窮本之論也。夫先王宰制羣動，役使萬物，固由於大禮之節，然非吾心之仁彌綸貫徹於其間，禮亦烏能以自行哉？是知爲國以禮，爲禮以仁，而領天下國家者，求仁之外無餘術也。不然，盛容飾繁，徒以滋侈；登降揖讓，祗以諧俗，而聖人制作之本窮矣。
translation_en:
…by which this accord is embodied? By uniting righteousness and accord to constitute benevolence, one can encompass all the goodness under Heaven. Could anyone who has attained this be inadequate to the responsibilities of an exalted position? Benevolence is an honored rank, through which one becomes the object of the multitude’s hopes. When it is practiced through righteousness, one’s conduct is fitting in every situation, and everyone under Heaven finds their proper place. Ascending the imperial throne on this basis, what cause could one still have for misgivings? Benevolence is a spacious dwelling, through which people’s hearts are drawn to allegiance. When it issues forth through accord, every measure is appropriate, and everyone under Heaven finds satisfaction in their feelings. Presiding as the great sovereign on this basis, would one not truly merit that designation? For where virtue resides, it can already embrace the vastness of Heaven and Earth; thus, where authority resides, one is naturally sufficient to possess what the sage treasures—the throne. Such indeed is the Way of embodying benevolence to lead others. What it encompasses is broad: embodying it brings together its entirety. The responsibility it bears is exalted: applying it fully realizes its subtle efficacy. This is why the Way of benevolence is great. When the former kings cultivated ritual to regulate human feelings, what foundation could they have had apart from benevolence?

Moreover, I have heard that there are three hundred principal rules of ritual and three thousand detailed observances, yet not a single matter among them is other than benevolence. This statement reaches to the very root. The former kings governed the manifold activities of living beings and directed the myriad things, certainly through the regulations of the great rites. Yet unless the benevolence within our hearts comprehensively informed and permeated them, how could ritual operate of itself? Thus we know that governing a state depends upon ritual, and practicing ritual depends upon benevolence. For those who preside over all under Heaven, states, and families, there is no other method beyond seeking benevolence. Otherwise, magnificent appearances and elaborate adornments merely encourage extravagance; ascending and descending, bowing and yielding merely conform to prevailing customs; and the foundation of the sages’ establishment of institutions is exhausted.

translation_en:
“Bringing forth in spring and fostering growth in summer are benevolence; gathering in autumn and storing in winter are righteousness. Benevolence is close to music; righteousness is close to ritual.”

Jiang Bin

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor: “The sages modeled themselves on Heaven and Earth in establishing ritual and music. This meaning is subtle, and examination candidates generally find it difficult to express. You may indeed be said to have accomplished this difficult task! Would it not be right to say that you understand the essential nature of ritual and music?”

Comment by Examiner Yuan, Expositor: “Lofty and well ordered.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Right Mentor: “Brings out the meaning of ‘close to.’”

The writer of the Record points out that the virtues of the transforming processes of nature accord with the institutions established by the sages. The sages harmonize their virtue with these transforming processes: how, then, could any gap separate benevolence and righteousness from ritual and music? The intention of the author of the Record of Music is to say that the sages take the transformations of Heaven and Earth as their model. Thus, in instituting ritual and music, the sages resemble Heaven and Earth and do not run counter to them.

Now, the movement of Heaven and Earth proceeds directly forward and spreads outward, and spring and summer run their courses through it. In spring, things are brought forth: all things joyfully unite and their transformations attain fullness. In summer, things are nurtured to maturity: all things flourish luxuriantly and develop freely. Is this not the benevolence of nature’s transforming processes? Benevolence as a virtue is the animating impulse through which things emerge. Thus, in their coming forth we see benevolence manifest itself, and in their growth we see benevolence flow and operate. In this way, the warm and generous virtue of Heaven and Earth can be understood.

text:
斂之物之性命各正矣冬則藏之物之太和保
合矣茲非造化之義乎蓋義之為德物之所由
以入機也于斂見義之利遂焉于藏見義之貞
固焉而天地尊嚴之德可識矣夫聖人本天地
以作樂則仁固樂之所從出也然仁以資天下
之生樂以宣天下之化其理實相孚焉是蓋仁
即無聲之樂而樂即有聲之仁顯微無間天人

translation_en:
…gathers them in, and the nature and allotted life of each thing are set right; in winter it stores them away, and their supreme harmony is preserved intact. Is this not the righteousness of the creative transformations of nature? For righteousness, as a virtue, is the pivotal agency through which things return inward. In gathering them in, we see righteousness bringing them to fruitful fulfillment; in storing them away, we see its steadfast firmness. Thus we may recognize the august dignity of Heaven and Earth’s virtue.

The sage bases himself upon Heaven and Earth in creating music, so benevolence is indeed the source from which music issues. Yet benevolence sustains the life of all under Heaven, while music gives expression to the transformation of all under Heaven: their principles truly accord. Benevolence is therefore music without sound, and music is benevolence with sound. Between the manifest and the subtle there is no separation; Heaven and humanity differ in their dispositions but share the same virtue. How could there be any distance between them?

The sage models himself upon nature’s creative transformations in establishing ritual, so righteousness is indeed the basis upon which ritual stands. Yet righteousness brings the nature of all under Heaven to fulfillment, while ritual regulates the feelings of all under Heaven: their workings truly depend upon one another. Righteousness is thus ritual without form, and ritual is righteousness embodied in form. They unite in an unfathomable unity; principle and vital force follow different courses but share the same source. Could they not be considered close to one another [?]?

Thus we know that in speaking of benevolence and righteousness, we encompass the spiritual transformations of Heaven and Earth; in speaking of ritual and music, we encompass the achievements and operations of the sage. Who but one who understands the Way could comprehend their unity? The Book of Changes says: “It is manifest in benevolence and concealed in its operations; it animates the myriad things without sharing the sage’s cares.” This means that Heaven and Earth accomplish transformation without conscious intention. The sage takes Heaven as his foundation and Earth as his model, employing ritual and music to regulate and give expression to all under Heaven. He thereby carries forward their Way, shaping and assisting its workings. Having matters that call for concern, he dares not imitate their freedom from care.

Nevertheless, when equilibrium and harmony are fully attained, and Heaven and Earth take their proper places and the myriad things receive nourishment; when ritual and music are practiced and the spirits arrive, then the sage…

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天之為心是惟以至虛者黙運其機焉耳然冲
漠之中無乎不具而至明之妙用自發見流行
而不已此天之所以為神也神故不測而化育
之著天下孰得以窮其原聖人為天之所獨厚
而合德乎天夫德與天合則心與天一是故體
備乎至虛而渾然萬理之畢具虛至而明亦至
而天下之善之幾悉統於聖人之心聖人以此
通人心之感而獨成其天而天下卒不能以窺
其妙然則聖人之心果有以大異乎天下而與
===
天同其神矣吾是以因朱子之言而知大舜之
心即天也蓋嘗稽諸天乎古之說天者莫辨矣
其曰維天之命於穆不已言精之運也其曰天
命流行物與無妄言誠之貫也其曰乾道變化
各正性命言賦之均也而天之所以為虛明者
未著也至曰混兮闢兮其無窮兮則有以善言
天之虛明矣夫混以涵其虛之體闢以闡其明
之用造化之神不於此而可見乎自今觀之乾
坤之蔵未發其蘊二五之化未彰其秘萬物之

之著天下孰得以窮其原聖人爲天之所獨厚
而合德乎天夫德與天合則心與天一是故體
備乎至虛而渾然萬理之畢具虛至而明亦至
而天下之善之幾悉統於聖人之心聖人以此
通人心之感而獨成其天而天下卒不能以窺
其妙然則聖人之心果有以大異乎天下而與
===
天同其神矣吾是以因孝子之言而知大舜之
心即天也蓋嘗稽諸天乎古之說天者莫辯矣
其曰維天之命於穆不已言精之運也其曰天
命流行物與無妄言誠之貫也其曰乾道變化
各正性命言賦之均也而天之所以爲虛明者
未著也至曰混兮闢兮其無窮兮則有以至言
天之虛明矣夫混以涵其虛之體闢以闡其明
之用造化之神不於此而可見乎自今觀之乾
坤之藏未發其蘊二五之化未彰其秘萬物之
punctuated:
天之為心，是惟以至虛者黙運其機焉耳。然冲漠之中，無乎不具，而至明之妙用，自發見流行而不已。此天之所以為神也。神故不測，而化育之著，天下孰得以窮其原？聖人為天之所獨厚，而合德乎天。夫德與天合，則心與天一。是故體備乎至虛，而渾然萬理之畢具；虛至而明亦至，而天下之善之幾，悉統於聖人之心。聖人以此通人心之感，而獨成其天，而天下卒不能以窺其妙。然則聖人之心，果有以大異乎天下，而與天同其神矣。吾是以因朱子之言，而知大舜之心即天也。
蓋嘗稽諸天乎？古之說天者，莫辨矣。其曰「維天之命，於穆不已」，言精之運也；其曰「天命流行，物與無妄」，言誠之貫也；其曰「乾道變化，各正性命」，言賦之均也。而天之所以為虛明者，未著也。至曰「混兮闢兮，其無窮兮」，則有以善言天之虛明矣。夫混以涵其虛之體，闢以闡其明之用，造化之神，不於此而可見乎？自今觀之，乾坤之蔵，未發其蘊；二五之化，未彰其秘；萬物之
translation_en:
…Heaven, in its activity as a mind, merely sets its workings silently in motion through utter emptiness. Yet within this stillness and silence nothing is lacking, and the wondrous operation of perfect clarity spontaneously manifests itself and flows without ceasing. This is what makes Heaven numinous. Being numinous, it is unfathomable; though its transforming and nurturing activity is manifest, who in the world can exhaustively trace its source? The sage receives Heaven’s especial bounty and accords with Heaven in virtue. When his virtue accords with Heaven, his mind is one with Heaven. Thus its substance is fully constituted in utter emptiness, while all principles are integrally present within it. When emptiness reaches perfection, clarity does likewise, and all the incipient stirrings of goodness under Heaven are encompassed within the sage’s mind. Through this he responds to the impulses of human minds and uniquely brings his Heaven-endowed nature to fulfillment, yet the world can never fathom his subtle workings. Thus the sage’s mind truly differs greatly from those of all others and shares Heaven’s numinous power. It is therefore through Master Zhu’s words that I know that the mind of the great Shun is Heaven itself.
Have we ever examined this in Heaven? Among those of antiquity who spoke of Heaven, none made the distinction clear [?]. The words, “Heaven’s mandate—ah, how profound and unceasing!” speak of the operation of its essential purity. The words, “Heaven’s mandate flows forth; things are endowed with freedom from falsity,” speak of the all-pervading character of sincerity. The words, “The Way of Qian changes and transforms, each thing attaining its proper nature and allotted destiny,” speak of the evenness of Heaven’s endowment. Yet what makes Heaven empty and clear has not been brought to light. Only with the words, “Undifferentiated! Opening forth! How inexhaustible!” is Heaven’s emptiness and clarity aptly expressed. In being undifferentiated, it contains the substance of its emptiness; in opening forth, it unfolds the operation of its clarity. Can we not see here the numinous power of creation and transformation? Viewed from this standpoint, what Qian and Kun hold in store has not yet unfolded its riches; the transformations of the two forces and the five phases have not yet disclosed their mysteries; the myriad things’ …

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
命未皙其幾時則天之爲心淵乎朕兆之莫窺
也杳乎機緘之弗露也湛乎其清通而不可象
也廓乎其無垠而不可執也渺乎其無方體而
不可求也而體之至虛立焉然至虛之中俯仰
畢備天之神明照知四方而絪縕綿亘何所不
及天之精粹作類萬物而洪纖幽顯何所不通
虛之立者明之生而其妙用之所著自昭布森
列而不容掩陰陽之慘舒也日月之晦朔也寒
暑之推遷也雨風露雷之變現也星辰經緯各
===
循其度山川融結各奠其維飛走草木各若其
生性情形體各順其軌端倪呈而法象立幾微
著而品物形而天地之化不亦至正而明達乎
是虛以受之明以出之不疾而自速不行而自
至而其所以然之故莫得而窮焉是天道之至
神也夫天生人而篤於聖聖人獨得其秀而最
靈者以合乎天而此心虛明之極默契其不測
之神吾見澄然其定而思慮之不萌也穆然其
靜而聞見之不淆也冲乎其入於玄而意必固

生性情形體各順其軌端倪呈而法象立幾微

靜而聞見之不滑也冲乎其入於玄而意必固
punctuated:
命未皙其幾，時則天之爲心，淵乎朕兆之莫窺也，杳乎機緘之弗露也，湛乎其清通而不可象也，廓乎其無垠而不可執也，渺乎其無方體而不可求也，而體之至虛立焉。然至虛之中，俯仰畢備。天之神明照知四方，而絪縕綿亘，何所不及？天之精粹作類萬物，而洪纖幽顯，何所不通？虛之立者，明之生，而其妙用之所著，自昭布森列而不容掩。陰陽之慘舒也，日月之晦朔也，寒暑之推遷也，雨風露雷之變現也，星辰經緯各循其度，山川融結各奠其維，飛走草木各若其生，性情形體各順其軌，端倪呈而法象立，幾微著而品物形，而天地之化不亦至正而明達乎？是虛以受之，明以出之，不疾而自速，不行而自至，而其所以然之故莫得而窮焉，是天道之至神也。
夫天生人而篤於聖，聖人獨得其秀而最靈者，以合乎天，而此心虛明之極，默契其不測之神。吾見澄然其定而思慮之不萌也，穆然其靜而聞見之不淆也，冲乎其入於玄而意必固
translation_en:
…the incipient workings of the life-endowments of the myriad things have not yet become clear. At such a time, Heaven as mind is so profound that no portent can be discerned, so remote that its hidden mechanism is not disclosed, so limpid in its clarity and unimpeded flow that it cannot be pictured, so expansive in its boundlessness that it cannot be grasped, and so vast, without fixed location or form, that it cannot be sought out. Thus its utterly empty substance is established. Yet within this utter emptiness, everything above and below is fully present. Heaven’s spiritual intelligence illuminates and knows the four quarters; its intermingling forces extend continuously—where do they not reach? Heaven’s pure essence brings forth the myriad things in their kinds; whether great or small, hidden or manifest—what does it not permeate? As emptiness is established, illumination arises. Wherever its wondrous operation becomes manifest, it spreads forth brightly in an ordered array that cannot be concealed. There are the severity and mildness of yin and yang, the dark and new-moon phases of the sun and moon, the alternation of cold and heat, and the changing manifestations of rain, wind, dew, and thunder. The stars, fixed and moving, each follow their proper courses; mountains and rivers, flowing and solidifying, each establish their sustaining framework. Flying and running creatures, grasses and trees each follow their manner of life; natures, feelings, forms, and bodies each follow their proper paths. The first signs appear and patterned images are established; subtle beginnings become manifest and the various things take shape. Are not the transformations of Heaven and Earth supremely correct, luminous, and unimpeded? Thus Heaven receives through emptiness and brings forth through illumination. Without haste it is swift of itself; without traveling it arrives of itself. Yet no one can exhaust the reason why this is so. This is the utmost spiritual efficacy of the Way of Heaven.
Heaven gives birth to human beings and bestows its richest gifts upon the sage. The sage alone receives what is most refined and spiritually responsive, thereby according with Heaven. In the utmost emptiness and illumination of his mind, he silently accords with Heaven’s unfathomable spiritual efficacy. I see his limpid settledness, in which deliberations have not yet sprouted; his solemn stillness, in which hearing and sight introduce no confusion; his profound emptiness as he enters the mysterious, with conjecture, insistence, obstinacy…

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
我之俱無也宥乎其隱於微而内外將迎之悉
泯也則亦天之虛而已矣虛則靈昭不昧之幾
發焉明覺自然之用行焉渾然者有以立其本
而粲然者所以逢其原存之則爲四德發之則
爲七情叙之則爲五倫章之則爲五服庸之則
爲五禮用之則爲五刑昭著之則爲六經宣布
之則爲萬化究極之則彌綸參贊中和位育之
能成焉感通之則天下一家中國一人之量充
焉而虛明之妙不與天並運而同神邪夫天地
===
儲精本真而靜而虛明之在吾心者固人人具
存也顧天下之爲心奪於習誘於物攻取於衆
欲壅閼於百私乃虛者汩焉明者翳焉而禀諸
天同諸聖者皆迷瞀而喪其初即返觀内照猶
憤憤然罔所覺睹矧欲其通天下之故邪聖人
以其所同乎天者達乎天下而道德性命并包
於中古今一息人物一身其幾皆具足於虛明
之奧是故聲入之則通物交之則化理觸之則
融機協之則順道同之則孚氣應之則適言與

我之俱無也，宥乎其隱於微而内外將迎之悉泯也，則亦天之虛而已矣。虛則靈昭不昧之幾發焉，明覺自然之用行焉。渾然者有以立其本，而粲然者所以逢其原。存之則爲四德，發之則爲七情，叙之則爲五倫，章之則爲五服，庸之則爲五禮，用之則爲五刑，昭著之則爲六經，宣布之則爲萬化。究極之則彌綸參贊、中和位育之能成焉，感通之則天下一家、中國一人之量充焉。而虛明之妙，不與天並運而同神邪？

translation_en:
…and self are all absent. Expansively [?], it withdraws into the subtle, and all inward and outward anticipation and reception disappear. This, too, is simply Heaven’s emptiness. Through emptiness, the incipient workings of undimmed spiritual illumination emerge, and the spontaneous operation of lucid awareness proceeds. Its undifferentiated wholeness establishes its foundation, while its brilliant differentiation gives access to its source. Preserved within, it constitutes the four virtues; expressed outwardly, the seven emotions; ordered, the five human relationships; manifested in distinctions, the five degrees of mourning dress; put into practice, the five rites; applied, the five punishments; clearly set forth, the Six Classics; disseminated, the myriad transformations. Pursued to its utmost, it achieves the capacity to encompass all things and assist Heaven and Earth, to bring about equilibrium and harmony, establish their proper positions, and nurture all beings. Through stimulus and response, it fully realizes the breadth of treating all under Heaven as one family and the Central Kingdom as one person. Does not the wondrous operation of emptiness and luminosity move together with Heaven and share its spiritual efficacy?
Heaven and Earth store up vital essence, fundamentally genuine and still; and the emptiness and luminosity within our minds are indeed present in everyone. Yet people’s minds are overpowered by habit, enticed by external things, assailed and captured by manifold desires, and obstructed by countless selfish concerns. Thus what was empty becomes muddied, and what was luminous becomes obscured. What they received from Heaven and share with the sages becomes wholly confused and loses its original state. Even if they turn their gaze inward and illuminate themselves, they remain troubled, perceiving nothing. How much less could they comprehend the workings of all under Heaven? Through what he shares with Heaven, the sage attains understanding of all under Heaven. title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
行諧之則從心所欲而不踰夫鑑誠空則不可
欺以天下之形衡誠平則不可爽以天下之物
聖人之心誠虛明則不可眩以天下之理如天
之於衆形匪物物而雕之而敦化川流並行並
育曷嘗不陳麗於其間邪是謂天之至神聖人
之至妙而稽古大舜則獨體其全焉蓋人心泯
乎其危也道心純乎其微也惟一則合乎天之
虛惟精則合乎天之明惟允中則合乎天之神
常寂常感常明常覺而大智所燭靡善不彰是
===
故好問好察而用中耕稼陶漁而取善則充其
虛明之度矣詢岳闢門而舍已達聰明目而同
人則溥其虛明之公矣去四凶而舉元凱命九
官而咨十二牧則廣其虛明之運矣由是而璣
衡齊政封山濬川則天地之心通焉由是而類
帝禋宗允若克諧則鬼神倫理之心通焉由是
而舞干風動鳳儀獸舞則民物夷狄之心通焉
而舜之至妙與天之至神一矣雖然精一執中
聖人達天之心學也後有作者舜其蔑以加矣

故好問好察而用中耕稼陶漁而取善則充其
虛明之度矣詢岳闢門而舍己逵聰明目而同

而舞干風動鳳儀獸舞則民物夷狄之心通焉
而舜之至妙與天之至神一矣雖然精一執中
聖人逹天之心學也後有作者舜其蔑以加矣
punctuated:
行諧之，則從心所欲而不踰。夫鑑誠空，則不可欺以天下之形；衡誠平，則不可爽以天下之物；聖人之心誠虛明，則不可眩以天下之理。如天之於衆形，匪物物而雕之，而敦化川流，並行並育，曷嘗不陳麗於其間邪？是謂天之至神，聖人之至妙。而稽古大舜，則獨體其全焉。蓋人心泯乎其危也，道心純乎其微也。惟一則合乎天之虛，惟精則合乎天之明，惟允中則合乎天之神。常寂常感，常明常覺，而大智所燭，靡善不彰。
是故好問好察而用中，耕稼陶漁而取善，則充其虛明之度矣；詢岳闢門而舍已，達聰明目而同人，則溥其虛明之公矣；去四凶而舉元凱，命九官而咨十二牧，則廣其虛明之運矣。由是而璣衡齊政，封山濬川，則天地之心通焉；由是而類帝禋宗，允若克諧，則鬼神倫理之心通焉；由是而舞干風動，鳳儀獸舞，則民物夷狄之心通焉。而舜之至妙與天之至神一矣。雖然，精一執中，聖人達天之心學也。後有作者，舜其蔑以加矣。
translation_en:
…when conduct accords with it, one follows the heart’s desires without overstepping the bounds. If a mirror is truly empty, no form in the world can deceive it; if a balance is truly level, no object in the world can cause it to err; if the sage’s heart is truly empty and luminous, no principle in the world can bewilder it. Consider Heaven’s relation to the myriad forms: it does not carve out each thing individually, yet its profound transforming power and its ceaseless flow operate together and nurture all things together. Are these not always displayed in their midst? This is called Heaven’s supreme spiritual efficacy and the sage’s supreme subtlety. Examining antiquity, we find that the great Shun alone embodied their entirety. The precariousness of the human heart was effaced, and the subtlety of the heart of the Way became pure. Singleness accords with Heaven’s emptiness; refinement accords with Heaven’s luminosity; truly holding to the mean accords with Heaven’s spiritual efficacy. Ever still and ever responsive, ever luminous and ever aware, his great wisdom illuminated all goodness, leaving none unmanifest.
Thus, by delighting in inquiry and close observation and putting the mean into practice, and by adopting what was good while ploughing, planting, making pottery, and fishing, he fulfilled the capacity of his empty and luminous heart. By consulting the Four Peaks and opening the gates of access, setting aside his own views [?], and by extending his hearing and sharpening his sight so as to act in accord with others, he spread its impartiality everywhere. By removing the Four Malefactors and promoting the Eight Yuan and Eight Kai, and by appointing the nine officials and consulting the twelve regional governors, he extended its operation. Through this, he used the jade astronomical instrument and its sighting tube to bring the celestial movements into order, raised altars on the mountains, and dredged the rivers, thereby attaining communion with the heart of Heaven and Earth. Through this, he offered the lei sacrifice to the Supreme Lord and pure sacrifices to the honored powers, achieving faithful accord and harmony, thereby attaining communion with the heart underlying spirits and human relationships. Through this, the dance with shields transformed people as the wind moves them, phoenixes came in stately procession, and beasts danced, thereby attaining communion with the hearts of the people, living creatures, and the Yi and Di peoples. Shun’s supreme subtlety thus became one with Heaven’s supreme spiritual efficacy. Nevertheless, refinement, singleness, and holding fast to the mean constitute the learning of the heart through which the sage reaches Heaven. Should another sage arise afterward, there would be nothing to add to Shun’s achievement.

punctuated:
御府之珍，睿藻傳神，驚覩化工之妙。既聞嘶而知德，亦持札而懷慙。臣誠惶誠恐，頓首頓首，上言：
伏念臣濂，雕蟲小夫，駑駘拙品。生當勝國之季，居在深山之中，竄形影以圖存，望風塵而增愾。著鞭首事，空憐祖逖之雄；歷塊非材，敢慕孫陽之遇？會真主崛興之始，正遺賢待出之時。過采虚名，至勤再三之驛召；曲承渥眷，親睹九五之龍飛。遂令徧歷于高華，未嘗少責以奔走。叨塵異數，首尾十年。感過隙之迅駒，漸空華髮；愧憑軒之衰鶴，恒抱汗顏。剪拂何施，馳驅難効。况乎三出三入，髀消乘傳之餘；兼以一節一趨，力匱登臺之後。嘆龍鍾之巳甚，瞻鳳閣而不前。豈期待廢之軀，翻軫益隆之顧？簡六閑之寶駿，羣無留良，
translation_en:
…a treasure from the imperial stables. Your sagely verse conveys its spirit: in amazement I behold the wonders of creation. Hearing its neigh, I recognize your benevolence; holding the written verses, I feel ashamed. Your servant, in deepest awe and fear, kowtows again and again and submits this memorial:
I humbly reflect that I, your servant Lian, am a petty practitioner of literary ornament, an inferior creature like a dull, slow horse. Born in the closing years of the former dynasty, I lived deep in the mountains, hiding myself to survive and gazing with growing anguish upon the dust of warfare. Taking up the whip to lead the undertaking, I could only admire Zu Ti’s heroism in vain; lacking the capacity to gallop over open ground, how could I dare aspire to recognition by Sun Yang, the judge of horses? The true sovereign’s rise coincided with the moment when overlooked worthy men awaited their emergence into service. You gave undue credit to my empty reputation, even taking the trouble to summon me repeatedly through the postal relay service. Favored beyond my deserts by your generous regard, I personally witnessed your dragon-like ascent to the imperial throne. You then allowed me to occupy a succession of illustrious posts, never exacting even a little toil in your service. Undeservedly enjoying these exceptional favors, I have passed ten years from beginning to end. Conscious that time speeds past like a swift colt glimpsed through a crack, I find my graying hair gradually thinning [?]; ashamed to resemble an aged crane riding in a grand carriage, I constantly blush at my unworthiness. What can your grooming and care accomplish for me, when I can scarcely repay you through exertion? Moreover, after three departures from court and three returns, my thighs have wasted away from journeys by relay carriage. And with each measured movement and hurried step [?], my strength is exhausted after ascending the terrace. Lamenting my extreme decrepitude, I gaze toward the Phoenix Pavilion but cannot advance. How could I have expected that this body, fit only to be set aside, would instead prompt your ever greater solicitude? You selected a precious steed from the six imperial stables, withholding none of the finest horses in the herd…

揮五色之雲篇，特將貌雅不重，懋德懋功之賞，忽臨私人私第之門。臣乃想容與于賦中，察風神于階下，得言得意而得象，掩周王黃澤之謡；和律和呂而和聲，陋漢帝蒲梢之曲。美而知愛，捧琬琰以驚心；感極生悲，撫樊纓而雪涕。一跌之虞可免，千官之眷誰先？
兹蓋伏遇皇帝陛下，冠古威神，御圖廣大，用三驅以取順，馳八駿以除殘。日月煥乎重明，乾坤帖爾再定。義降江表，畢收倚馬之才；詔下域中，至有墜驢之笑。駕馭一時之豪傑，廓清萬里之妖氛。有如愚臣，亦冒殊獎。彼奇才之蘇子，甘為前驅；若安國之康侯，尤當退舍。何悟一朝之錫，仰同二氏之榮？鳳臆龍鬐，攷馬經而待異，過堤趨
translation_en:
…You wielded your brush to compose a cloudlike text of five colors, specially bestowing something of elegant appearance and little weight [?]; a reward for eminent virtue and achievement suddenly arrived at the gate of your servant’s private residence. Your servant then imagined the horse’s leisurely grace through the rhapsody and observed its spirited bearing below the steps. Capturing its expression, meaning, and image, the composition eclipses the Zhou king’s Song of Huangze; harmonizing the pitch standards, both yang and yin, and bringing the sounds into concord, it makes the Han emperor’s Song of Pushao seem crude. Recognizing its beauty, I cherish it; holding the jade-like composition, I am overwhelmed. Gratitude at its height turns to sorrow; stroking the breast straps and tassels, I wipe away my tears. I may now escape the danger of a fall: among the thousand officials, who has received such favor before me?
This is because I have humbly encountered Your Majesty the Emperor, whose divine majesty surpasses antiquity and whose imperial designs are vast. You employ the hunt with three sides driven to secure willing submission, and send forth the eight steeds to eliminate the cruel. Sun and moon shine with renewed brilliance; Heaven and Earth are peacefully settled once more. Your righteousness descends upon the lands south of the Yangtze [?], gathering all those talented enough to compose while leaning against a horse; your edicts issue throughout the realm, even occasioning the laughter of one falling from his donkey. You direct the heroes of the age and clear away baleful influences across ten thousand li. Even a foolish servant such as I has received your exceptional reward. That remarkably talented Master Su would willingly ride ahead; even Lord Kang, who brought peace to the state, would have to yield precedence. How could I have imagined that a single day’s bestowal would confer upon me an honor equal to that of these two men? With a phoenix’s breast and a dragon’s mane, the horse is judged exceptional by the Classic of Horses [?]; crossing the embankment, it hastens toward…

闕，從人欲而不違，乃知大宛之種非凡，而益信王者之言有驗也。所媿難報者德，但徒懷裹革之思；不待者年，亦無多據鞍之日。第當勉尋舊學，堅保初忠。踐霜雪而全身，無羨莊生之論；當晚暮而求道，庶覿齊主之知。伏願朽索馭民，兼金賈士，永定萬年之軌，先登九方之明。華山之戰騎咸歸，在在歌鎬君之德；黄河之瑞圖忽出，煌煌表羲后之靈。臣無任瞻天仰聖、激切屏營之至，謹奉表稱謝以聞。

translation_en:
…the palace gates, complying with human wishes without resistance. Thus I know that the stock of Dayuan is extraordinary, and believe all the more that a king’s words prove true. What shames me is your beneficence, which I can scarcely repay: I can only cherish the resolve to return wrapped in horsehide after dying in battle. The years will not wait, and few days remain for me to sit in the saddle. I must simply strive to revisit my former learning and steadfastly preserve my original loyalty. Treading frost and snow while keeping myself whole, I need not envy what Master Zhuang describes; seeking the way in my declining years, I hope to meet with recognition like that accorded by the ruler of Qi to an old horse’s knowledge of the road.
I humbly wish that you may govern the people as cautiously as though holding rotten reins, and recruit worthy men with gold of double value; establish forever the course of rule for ten thousand years, and surpass even Jiufang in discerning excellence in horses. May all the warhorses be turned loose on Mount Hua, with songs everywhere praising the virtue of the sovereign of Hao; may an auspicious chart suddenly emerge from the Yellow River, brilliantly displaying the numinous power of the sovereign Fuxi. Gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your Sagely Majesty, your servant cannot contain his fervent emotion and trembling awe. I respectfully submit this memorial to express my gratitude and make it known to Your Majesty.

第一問
鄭時平

同考試官教諭丁批：我皇上之壽配天無疆，超越前聖，天下臣民皆竊窺而謳吟之。是作揄揚稱頌，而忠愛之意甚篤，其效華封之祝者乎？

translation_en:
First Policy Question
Zheng Shiping

Comment by Associate Examiner Ding, Instructor: Our Emperor’s longevity matches Heaven’s boundlessness and surpasses that of earlier sages. All officials and common people throughout the realm humbly glimpse it and sing its praises. This composition extols and celebrates it, expressing profound loyalty and affection. Does it not emulate the blessings offered by the border warden of Hua?

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, metropolitan graduate (jinshi): Our Emperor accords above with Heaven’s heart and receives its boundless favor and protection because of his consummate virtue and wondrous Way. You can investigate and expound these, striving to uncover their subtleties; you cannot be regarded as an ordinary scholar from the wilds.

text:
皇上之德又克當乎
天心此所以保定孔固而
萬壽無疆也祝願之詞諸士皆有至能言天人相與之際者獨此作得焉錄之
聖人之道天道也天不息聖人之道亦不
息夫不息者氣之所以達也聖人之德天
德也天無心聖人之德亦無心夫無心者
神之所以定也神定則固氣達則暢暢則
順順則利利則無所不治五內皆融六府

徒與造物爲徒則亦與造物爲壽天地一

固若是也然不知者衆彼不知者難以語

聖人之道，天道也。天不息，聖人之道亦不息。夫不息者，氣之所以達也。聖人之德，天德也。天無心，聖人之德亦無心。夫無心者，神之所以定也。神定則固，氣達則暢，暢則順，順則利，利則無所不治，五內皆融，六府皆和矣。固則靜，靜則虛，虛則無所不照，萬化自歸，萬物自正矣。夫皆融皆和，自歸自正，夫是之謂弗擾。弗擾之謂弗勞，弗勞之謂得一。夫一也者，天以是清，地以是寧，聖人以是治天下。天地悠久，聖人亦悠久；天地無疆，聖人亦無疆。夫是之謂與造物爲徒。與造物爲徒，則亦與造物爲壽。天地一聖人，聖人一天地，未有兩焉者也，亦其理固若是也。然不知者衆，彼不知者難以語道，又可以語壽邪？愚嘗求之千萬世之前，
translation_en:
…His Majesty’s virtue, moreover, fully accords with Heaven’s intent. This is why his security is so firmly assured and his longevity knows no bounds. All the candidates offer words of blessing; but this composition alone succeeds in expressing the workings of the relationship between Heaven and humanity. I have selected it for inclusion.

The Way of the sage is the Way of Heaven. Heaven never ceases, and the Way of the sage likewise never ceases. This ceaselessness is what enables vital energy to circulate freely. The virtue of the sage is the virtue of Heaven. Heaven acts without a deliberate mind, and the virtue of the sage likewise operates without a deliberate mind. This absence of deliberate intent is what enables the spirit to become settled. When the spirit is settled, it becomes firm; when vital energy circulates freely, it flows unimpeded. Unimpeded flow brings harmony; harmony brings ease; ease leaves nothing out of proper order. The five inner organs are all in accord, and the six viscera are all in harmony. Firmness brings stillness; stillness brings emptiness; emptiness leaves nothing unilluminated. The myriad transformations return of themselves to their source, and the myriad things rectify themselves. This universal accord and harmony, this spontaneous return and rectification, are called freedom from disturbance. Freedom from disturbance is called freedom from toil; freedom from toil is called attaining the One. Through this One, Heaven is clear, Earth is tranquil, and the sage governs all under Heaven. Heaven and Earth endure, and the sage likewise endures; Heaven and Earth know no bounds, and the sage likewise knows no bounds. This is called being a companion of the Creator. To be a companion of the Creator is also to share the Creator’s longevity. Heaven and Earth are a single sage; the sage is a single Heaven and Earth. They have never been two separate entities: their underlying principle is inherently thus. Yet many do not understand. If it is difficult to speak of the Way to those who do not understand, how could one speak to them of longevity? I, in my humble understanding, have sought this among the thousands and myriads of generations of the distant past…

Their Way and virtue alike never extended beyond revering Heaven and caring for the people; their effects ultimately lay in freely flowing vital energy and a settled spirit. …following without ruling over them, according with the ordering of Heaven and Earth, and allowing the dispositions of all things to find fulfillment: that was all. Thus Yao’s vital energy was always freely circulating, and his spirit always settled. He reigned for ninety-eight years and lived to the age of one hundred and seventeen. The Canon of Shun records Emperor Shun’s conduct of government. In his actions, Shun used the astronomical instruments to bring the celestial regulators into alignment, opened the four gates to make understanding flow freely, displayed his might by campaigning against the Miao, and spread his beneficence by increasing material resources. title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
三言者其指雖殊然其道即爲而不有順
而不宰之說也何以解焉蓋一也者言乎
其心也圓徹靈覺上與太虚其竅流通渾
爲一體斯之謂一也和也者言乎其德也
靜與天合不失吾本動與人合不失吾常
斯之謂和也寧也者言乎其志也靜也固
靜動也亦靜無靜無動無終無始斯之謂
寧也一者不擾則萬化自順和者不滯則
衆物皆軌寧者不摇則百昌咸遂故曰一
===

不宰之說也故人之爲言也言天而天言
地而地邈不相通聖人之爲言也言天則
無地言地則無天一貫之道也不可不察
也於戲黄帝堯舜去遠矣愚所論者特求
之聲跡文字之遺而因推其精神心術之
奥未能身睹之也今愚幸而身睹
聖天子之行政矣又身睹其
壽矣其行政一皆法天之不息以爲道體天之

…these three expressions, though different in their purport, convey the same Way as the teaching of acting without possessing and following without dominating. How can this be explained? Unity refers to the heart-mind. Perfectly penetrating and spiritually aware, its apertures communicate above with the Great Void, merging into a single whole: this is what is called unity. Harmony refers to virtue. In stillness, one accords with Heaven without losing one’s fundamental nature; in movement, one accords with others without losing one’s constant principles: this is what is called harmony. Tranquillity refers to the will. In stillness, it is indeed still; in movement, it is also still. There is neither stillness nor movement, neither end nor beginning: this is what is called tranquillity. When unity is undisturbed, the myriad transformations proceed naturally in due order; when harmony is unobstructed, all things follow their proper course; when tranquillity is unshaken, all living things attain fulfilment. Thus I say that unity, harmony, and tranquillity—these three expressions—convey the teaching of acting without possessing and following without dominating. When ordinary people speak, their talk of Heaven concerns Heaven alone, and their talk of Earth concerns Earth alone: the two remain remote and unconnected. When sages speak, their talk of Heaven leaves no separate Earth, and their talk of Earth leaves no separate Heaven. This is the Way that runs through all as one; it must be examined carefully.

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
嘗離次也是故以
氣則恒達焉以
神則恒定焉以
壽則長乆而不知所極焉然而在
廷諸臣皆以我
皇上之壽不獨兼總三聖而直至萬年者則固
有卜焉蓋黃帝之所爲壽者一若和而已
堯舜之所爲壽者寧而已各殊其德而不
能相兼也愚嘗竊讀我
===
皇上敬一之箴矣其曰勿參以三勿貳以二者
則與黃帝和一之指同其曰清淨虛無欲日
新不已者則與堯舜出寧之指同夫彼三
聖人者人抱一德且得年甚永今我
皇上蓋兼三聖人之德而統會之矣愚聞之道
什于人者壽什于人德百于人者壽百于
人唯我
皇上道什于軒轅而德百于唐虞諸臣所謂有
萬年之筭者用是道卜之也雖然天無心生聖

punctuated: 嘗離次也。是故以氣則恒達焉，以神則恒定焉，以壽則長乆而不知所極焉。然而在廷諸臣皆以我皇上之壽不獨兼總三聖而直至萬年者，則固有卜焉。蓋黃帝之所爲壽者，一若和而已；堯舜之所爲壽者，寧而已。各殊其德，而不能相兼也。愚嘗竊讀我皇上《敬一》之箴矣。其曰「勿參以三，勿貳以二」者，則與黃帝和一之指同；其曰「清淨虛無，欲日新不已」者，則與堯舜出寧之指同。夫彼三聖人者，人抱一德，且得年甚永；今我皇上蓋兼三聖人之德而統會之矣。愚聞之：道什于人者，壽什于人；德百于人者，壽百于人。唯我皇上道什于軒轅，而德百于唐虞。諸臣所謂有萬年之筭者，用是道卜之也。雖然，天無心，生聖
translation_en:
…has never departed from its station. Thus, in vital energy, he is ever unimpeded; in spirit, ever settled; and in longevity, enduring beyond any known limit. Yet the ministers at court all hold that our Emperor’s lifespan will not merely encompass those of the three sages combined, but will extend to ten thousand years; they certainly have grounds for this prediction. For Huangdi’s longevity arose only from unity and harmony [?], while Yao’s and Shun’s arose only from tranquility. Each possessed his distinctive virtue, without being able to combine it with the others.

I have humbly read our Emperor’s Admonition on Revering the One (Jingyi). Its words, “Do not mingle it with three; do not divide it with two,” accord with Huangdi’s purport of harmony and unity. Its words, “Purity, tranquility, emptiness, and absence; desire daily renewal without cease” [?], accord with Yao’s and Shun’s purport of bringing forth tranquility [?]. Each of those three sages possessed a single virtue and nevertheless attained a very long life. Now our Emperor possesses the virtues of all three sages and unites them into one whole.

I have heard that one whose Way is ten times that of others enjoys ten times their longevity, and one whose virtue is a hundred times that of others enjoys a hundred times their longevity. Our Emperor alone surpasses Xuanyuan tenfold in the Way, and Tang Yao and Yu Shun a hundredfold in virtue. When the ministers speak of his allotted lifespan of ten thousand years, they base their prediction on this principle. Nevertheless, Heaven has no conscious intent, yet brings forth sages…

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
人有心天無爲托聖人有爲故聖人之生
也必受之異焉必厚之周焉必助之至焉
聖人之壽殆天乎何說乎受之異也夫人
生等氣耳唯聖人靜之若山動之若川上
知千歲下知千歲也故曰壽者受也謂受
之異也何說乎厚之周也其所居鉤陳衛
座虎豹守關天降甘露以悅其志地產嘉
禾以昭其德故曰壽者厚也謂厚之周也
何說乎助之至也忽不意老人獻雉羹焉
===
山人呼萬歲焉未有所作鬼神將告之一
有所思鬼神將啓之故曰壽者助也謂助
之至也由此言之我
皇上之壽非天而何哉愚也生在蒿蓬之野而
游乎甸服之中觀
聖人之治而不究其道被
聖人之化而不測其德頌
聖人之壽而不知其要領之所在唯執事教焉
第二問

===
皇上之壽非天而何哉愚也生在蒿蓬之野而
游乎甸服之中觀
聖人之治而不究其道被
聖人之化而不測其德頌
聖人之壽而不知其要領之所在唯執事教焉
第二問
punctuated:
人有心，天無爲，托聖人有爲。故聖人之生也，必受之異焉，必厚之周焉，必助之至焉。聖人之壽，殆天乎！何說乎受之異也？夫人生等氣耳，唯聖人靜之若山，動之若川，上知千歲，下知千歲也。故曰：「壽者，受也。」謂受之異也。何說乎厚之周也？其所居，鉤陳衛座，虎豹守關，天降甘露以悅其志，地產嘉禾以昭其德。故曰：「壽者，厚也。」謂厚之周也。何說乎助之至也？忽不意老人獻雉羹焉，山人呼萬歲焉。未有所作，鬼神將告之；一有所思，鬼神將啓之。故曰：「壽者，助也。」謂助之至也。由此言之，我皇上之壽，非天而何哉！愚也生在蒿蓬之野，而游乎甸服之中，觀聖人之治而不究其道，被聖人之化而不測其德，頌聖人之壽而不知其要領之所在，唯執事教焉。

第二問
translation_en:
…sages possess intention. Heaven acts without deliberate effort, entrusting deliberate action to sages. Thus, when a sage is born, he must receive an exceptional endowment, be blessed with comprehensive bounty, and receive assistance in the highest degree. Surely a sage’s longevity comes from Heaven! What is meant by receiving an exceptional endowment? All people are born with vital energy alike; only the sage is still as a mountain and moves like a river, knowing a thousand years into the past and a thousand years into the future. Thus it is said: “Longevity (shou) means receiving (shou).” This refers to the exceptional endowment he receives. What is meant by being blessed with comprehensive bounty? Where he dwells, Gouchen guards his throne, and tigers and leopards guard his gates. Heaven sends down sweet dew to delight his heart, and the earth produces auspicious grain to manifest his virtue. Thus it is said: “Longevity means bounty.” This refers to the comprehensiveness of that bounty. What is meant by receiving assistance in the highest degree? Suddenly and unexpectedly, an old man presents pheasant broth, and mountain dwellers cry, “May you live ten thousand years!” Before he undertakes anything, spirits will notify him; as soon as he conceives a thought, spirits will enlighten him. Thus it is said: “Longevity means assistance.” This refers to assistance in the highest degree. From this we may say: if our Emperor’s longevity does not come from Heaven, whence could it come? I, in my ignorance, was born in the countryside amid wormwood and brush, yet now travel within the royal domain. I observe the sage’s government without fathoming his Way; I receive the sage’s transforming influence without comprehending his virtue; I praise the sage’s longevity without knowing wherein its essentials lie. I ask only that you instruct me.

Second Question

法之趨於敝也唯智士爲能酌其宜法之
===
趨於窮也唯聖人爲能通其變蓋天下無
不敝之法而捄之者不酌其宜則其敝愈
滋矣天下亦無不窮之法而濟之者不通
其變則其窮益甚矣智士憂時憫國不忍
其敝之滋也慨然建議而捄之周思其利
害稽察其情僞劑量其事機之輕重必使
權操於上而法行於下國與民均賴其福
焉是之謂因敝補偏以佐國家之急權一

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
物變化法久而窮窮則通之以變意嚮所
在天下改易觀聽而從欲焉故令之則行
禁之則止神化鼓舞而民不倦矣是之謂
裁成輔相以左右民立百王之法也此錢
幣之制賈誼劉秩孔顗諸臣條列於前皆
不失爲經國之智而我
皇上洞照積習之弊一旦滌惡錢之蒐慝折其
中而新之超軼千古兼總三臣之說而通
變以宜其民非所謂
===
聖人盡制而不私邪請悉陳之以復明問夫自
燧人氏以輕重爲天下而錢之法始興自
禹湯以歷山莊山之金鑄幣而錢之法寖
具然而用之廣猶未也至太公立九府圜
法而錢始流布於天下自兹而降民無錢
不用貨無錢不售而錢之權顧出於布帛
穀粟之上而天下之物莫不準之以低昂
矣何者天下百貨皆資錢以流通重者不
可舉非錢不能以致遠滯者不能達非錢
alt_text:
物變化法乂而窮窮則通之以變意嚮所
在天下改易觀聽而從欲焉故令之則行
禁之則止神化鼓舞而民不倦矣是之謂
裁成輔相以左右民百王之法也此錢
幣之制賈誼劉秩孔顗諸臣條列於前皆
不失爲經國之智而我
皇上洞照積習之弊一旦滌惡錢之蒐慝折其
中而新之超軼千古兼總三臣之說而通
變以宜其民非所謂
===
聖人盡制而不私邪請悉陳之以復明問夫自
燧人氏以輕重爲天下而錢之法始興自
禹湯以歷山莊山之金鑄幣而錢之法寖
具然而用之廣猶未也至太公立九府圜
法而錢始流布於天下自茲而降民無錢
不用貨無錢不售而錢之權顧出於布帛
穀粟之上而天下之物莫不準之以低昂
矣何者天下百貨皆資錢以流通重者不
可舉非錢不能以致遠滯者不能達非錢
punctuated:
物變化，法久而窮，窮則通之以變。意嚮所在，天下改易觀聽而從欲焉。故令之則行，禁之則止，神化鼓舞而民不倦矣。是之謂裁成輔相以左右民，立百王之法也。此錢幣之制，賈誼、劉秩、孔顗諸臣條列於前，皆不失爲經國之智。而我皇上洞照積習之弊，一旦滌惡錢之蒐慝，折其中而新之，超軼千古，兼總三臣之說而通變以宜其民，非所謂聖人盡制而不私邪？請悉陳之，以復明問。
夫自燧人氏以輕重爲天下，而錢之法始興；自禹湯以歷山、莊山之金鑄幣，而錢之法寖具。然而用之廣，猶未也。至太公立九府圜法，而錢始流布於天下。自兹而降，民無錢不用，貨無錢不售，而錢之權顧出於布帛穀粟之上，而天下之物莫不準之以低昂矣。何者？天下百貨，皆資錢以流通。重者不可舉，非錢不能以致遠；滯者不能達，非錢
translation_en:
…and changes in response to things. When institutions, long established, reach an impasse, he opens a way through by changing them. Wherever his intentions are directed, all under Heaven alter what they see and hear and follow his wishes. Thus, when he commands, they act; when he prohibits, they stop. Through wondrous transformation he inspires the people, and they do not grow weary. This is what is meant by shaping and assisting the processes of nature to guide the people, establishing institutions for a hundred generations of kings. As for this system of coinage, the proposals previously set out by such ministers as Jia Yi, Liu Zhi, and Kong Yi all exemplified wisdom in ordering the state. Yet our Emperor has thoroughly discerned the abuses of entrenched practices and, at a stroke, swept away the accumulated evils of debased coinage [?]. By striking the proper balance and renewing the system, he has surpassed all antiquity. He has brought together the arguments of these three ministers and adapted them through change to benefit his people. Is this not what is meant by the sage fully establishing institutions without partiality? Allow me to set this out in full in response to your illuminating question.
When Sui Ren governed all under Heaven through the balancing of relative values, the system of money first arose. When Yu and Tang cast currency from the metal of Mount Li and Mount Zhuang, the system gradually took fuller shape. Yet its use was still not widespread. Only when Tai Gong established the monetary regulations of the Nine Treasuries did money begin to circulate throughout the realm. Thereafter, there was no money the people did not use, and no commodity that could be sold without money. Money’s power consequently rose above that of cloth, silk, and grain, and everything under Heaven took it as the standard by which its value rose or fell. Why was this? All the realm’s many commodities depend upon money for their circulation. Heavy goods cannot be carried readily; without money, they cannot be conveyed to distant places. Goods held up cannot circulate; without money…

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
不能以兼濟大者不可分非錢不得以小
用金銀之屬細用之則耗組織之文片析
之則廢惟鑄銅以爲錢物多則稱其多物
少則稱其少灌輸交易簡便不煩物價平
而爭奪寡彼我均而權算明錢幣之在天
下與民相倚依爲命即一日不可廢也然
鼓鑄之權在上而不在下上之人以義制
利獨操握之而不使之冒禁以作奸則天
下之人不罹其害而蒙其利矣是私鑄之
===
令聖王必嚴爲之防自古迄今未之有改
也已矣何賢君如漢文帝而欲放鑄以予
民賈誼憂其禍之博也於是有七福之說
賢相如張九齡而請縱民之自鑄劉秩患
其行之必不可也於是乎有四美之規儒
臣杜佑亟稱二子之論詳旨而達其要焉
夫誼之七福何也黥罪不積一矣偽錢不
蕃民不相疑二矣采銅鑄作者返之耕田
三矣上挾銅積以御輕重貨物必平四矣

下之人不罹其害而蒙其利矣是私鑄之
===
令聖王必嚴爲之防自古迄今未之有改
也已矣何賢君如漢文帝而欲放鑄以予
民賈誼憂其禍之博也於是有七福之說
賢相如張九齡而請縱民之自鑄劉秩患
其行之必不可也於是乎有四美之規儒
臣杜佑亟稱二子之論詳旨而達其要焉
夫誼之七福何也黥罪不積一矣僞錢不
蓄民不相疑二矣采銅鑄作者返之耕田
三矣上挾銅積以御輕重貨物必平四矣
punctuated:
不能以兼濟；大者不可分，非錢不得以小用。金銀之屬，細用之則耗；組織之文，片析之則廢。惟鑄銅以爲錢，物多則稱其多，物少則稱其少，灌輸交易，簡便不煩。物價平而爭奪寡，彼我均而權算明。錢幣之在天下，與民相倚依爲命，即一日不可廢也。然鼓鑄之權在上而不在下，上之人以義制利，獨操握之，而不使之冒禁以作奸，則天下之人不罹其害而蒙其利矣。是私鑄之令，聖王必嚴爲之防，自古迄今，未之有改也已矣。
何賢君如漢文帝，而欲放鑄以予民？賈誼憂其禍之博也，於是有七福之說。賢相如張九齡，而請縱民之自鑄？劉秩患其行之必不可也，於是乎有四美之規。儒臣杜佑亟稱二子之論詳旨而達其要焉。
夫誼之七福何也？黥罪不積，一矣；偽錢不蕃，民不相疑，二矣；采銅鑄作者返之耕田，三矣；上挾銅積以御輕重，貨物必平，四矣。
translation_en:
…cannot be made available wherever needed without money; large objects cannot be divided, and without money cannot serve for small purchases. Gold and silver suffer loss when used in small portions; patterned woven fabrics are ruined when cut into pieces. Only copper cast into coins allows payment to match a large quantity of goods or a small one. Circulation and exchange are simple and convenient, without complications. Prices remain equitable and contention diminishes; both parties receive their due, and weighing and reckoning are clear. Money throughout the realm and the people depend upon one another for their existence: it cannot be dispensed with for even a single day. Yet authority over minting belongs to those above, not those below. If those above regulate profit through righteousness, retain sole control of this authority, and prevent people from violating prohibitions to commit fraud, then the people throughout the realm will escape its harms and enjoy its benefits. Thus, regarding the regulation of private minting, sage kings invariably impose strict safeguards. From antiquity to the present, this has never changed.
Why, then, did even so worthy a ruler as Emperor Wen of Han wish to open minting to the people? Jia Yi feared the far-reaching harm this would cause, and therefore advanced his account of seven blessings. Why did even so worthy a chief minister as Zhang Jiuling request that the people be allowed to mint coins themselves? Liu Zhi feared that this proposal could never be practicable, and therefore offered his admonition concerning four benefits. The Confucian official Du You repeatedly praised these two men’s arguments for their detailed exposition and grasp of the essentials.
What were Jia Yi’s seven blessings? Offenses punishable by tattooing would not multiply: that was the first. Counterfeit coins would not proliferate, and people would not distrust one another: that was the second. Those mining copper and casting coins would return to cultivating the fields: that was the third. Those above would control accumulated copper to regulate relative values, ensuring equitable prices for goods: that was the fourth. …

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
作兵器假貴臣多少有制五矣臨萬貨調
盈虛收奇羨六矣制吾棄財與匈奴逐爭
其民七矣是皆斟酌機權卓有定識誼真
通達國體者乎秩之四美何也銅不布下
而盜鑄者無因一也公錢不破二也人不
犯死刑三也錢貨日增四也是皆揣盡情
弊確有遠慮秩真深究利源者乎二子之
後論錢法者代相隨屬而南齊孔覬則推
原盜鑄之禍深而嚴法不能禁者由上人
===
之惜銅愛工也先臣丘濬歎服覬之兩言
爲萬世鑄錢不易之良法焉夫銅擅於官
而無所惜則體質厚而肉好適均工出於
上而無所愛則製作精而輪郭周正本多
而費重工倍而力艱即驅民使鑄亦將不
爲矣況冒禁犯法而盜爲之哉是七福四
美所以操其公鑄之柄而不惜銅愛工者
所以杜其私鑄之奸三子之言互相發明
有國家者采而施行之則錢之爲利不足

所以杜其私鑄之奸三子之言互相發明
有國家者采而施行之則錢之爲利不足
punctuated: 作兵器、假貴臣，多少有制，五矣；臨萬貨，調盈虛，收奇羨，六矣；制吾棄財，與匈奴逐爭其民，七矣。是皆斟酌機權，卓有定識，誼真通達國體者乎！秩之四美何也？銅不布下，而盜鑄者無因，一也；公錢不破，二也；人不犯死刑，三也；錢貨日增，四也。是皆揣盡情弊，確有遠慮，秩真深究利源者乎！二子之後，論錢法者代相隨屬，而南齊孔覬則推原盜鑄之禍深而嚴法不能禁者，由上人之惜銅愛工也。先臣丘濬歎服覬之兩言，爲萬世鑄錢不易之良法焉。夫銅擅於官而無所惜，則體質厚而肉好適均；工出於上而無所愛，則製作精而輪郭周正。本多而費重，工倍而力艱，即驅民使鑄，亦將不爲矣，況冒禁犯法而盜爲之哉！是七福四美，所以操其公鑄之柄；而不惜銅愛工者，所以杜其私鑄之奸。三子之言，互相發明。有國家者采而施行之，則錢之爲利不足
translation_en:
…The quantities used to make weapons or lent to high ministers would be regulated: this is the fifth benefit. The government would oversee all commodities, adjust surpluses and shortages, and absorb exceptional surpluses: this is the sixth. By controlling our otherwise unused resources, we could compete with the Xiongnu to attract their people: this is the seventh. All these proposals weigh circumstances and expedients and display remarkably firm judgment. Was not Jia Yi truly versed in the essentials of government!

What were Liu Zhi’s four advantages? Copper would not circulate among the populace, leaving illicit coiners without the means to operate: this is the first. Official coins would not be broken up: this is the second. People would not incur the death penalty: this is the third. The supply of coin would increase daily: this is the fourth. All these proposals thoroughly assess the circumstances and abuses and show sound foresight. Did not Liu Zhi truly investigate the sources of economic benefit in depth!

After these two men, discussions of monetary policy continued from generation to generation. Kong Ji of the Southern Qi traced the underlying reason why illicit minting caused such grave harm yet could not be stopped by stringent laws: those above were sparing with copper and unwilling to expend labor. The late minister Qiu Jun admired these two observations of Kong Ji, regarding them as sound principles of coinage that would remain valid for all ages.

If copper is controlled exclusively by the authorities and used unstintingly, coins will be substantial in thickness, with their metal bodies and central holes properly proportioned. If labor is provided by those above and expended unstintingly, workmanship will be fine, and rims and borders will be uniformly regular. With substantial capital requirements and heavy expenses, twice the labor and arduous exertion, even if people were driven to mint coins, they would be unwilling to do so. How much less would they risk violating prohibitions and breaking the law to mint them illicitly!

Thus, the seven benefits and four advantages explain how to retain control of official minting, while unstinting expenditure of copper and labor prevents the abuses of private minting. The statements of these three men illuminate one another. If those who govern a state adopt and implement them, would not the benefits of coinage suffice to…

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以通融兼濟而致府庫之充實國計之有
儲哉洪惟
聖祖開基初置寶源局鑄大中通寶與歷代錢
兼行之洪武六年禁民間私鑄鑄者許作
廢銅入官而更造焉
成祖
列聖皆有年號通寶而嚴盜鑄之禁則申著律
令炳炳如丹百八十年以来法重而人不
敢犯錢行而人莫之撓所謂良法美意經
===
久詳密宜萬世相循守之無弊也奈之何
法久不能不窮法窮不能不變通其變以
濟天下之窮制其義以公天下之利寧無
待於
聖天子乎我
皇上稽乾履泰建極開人明備禮樂追琢紀綱
道揆而法守懷刑而信度
中興之鴻烈昭登顯定焯焯乎榮鏡宇宙無
競也顧宏規上儀既皆底績而物宜民用

久詳宻宜萬世相循守之無弊也柰之何

待於

中興之鴻烈昭登顯定焯焯乎縈鏡宇宙無
競也顧宏規上儀既皆底績而物宜民用
punctuated:
以通融兼濟，而致府庫之充實、國計之有儲哉？洪惟聖祖開基，初置寶源局，鑄大中通寶，與歷代錢兼行之。洪武六年，禁民間私鑄，鑄者許作廢銅入官而更造焉。成祖、列聖皆有年號通寶，而嚴盜鑄之禁，則申著律令，炳炳如丹。百八十年以来，法重而人不敢犯，錢行而人莫之撓。所謂良法美意，經久詳密，宜萬世相循守之無弊也。
奈之何，法久不能不窮，法窮不能不變。通其變以濟天下之窮，制其義以公天下之利，寧無待於聖天子乎？我皇上稽乾履泰，建極開人，明備禮樂，追琢紀綱，道揆而法守，懷刑而信度。中興之鴻烈，昭登顯定，焯焯乎榮鏡宇宙，無競也。顧宏規上儀既皆底績，而物宜民用
translation_en:
…to facilitate circulation and provide assistance to all, thereby filling the treasuries and ensuring reserves for state expenditure? Reverently we recall that when the Sagely Founder established the dynasty, he first set up the Coinage Office (Baoyuan ju), casting Dazhong tongbao coins to circulate alongside the coinage of previous dynasties. In the sixth year of Hongwu, private minting among the people was prohibited; coins thus cast could be surrendered to the authorities as scrap copper and recast. Chengzu and the succeeding sage emperors all issued tongbao coins bearing their reign titles. To enforce the prohibition against illicit minting, they reiterated it expressly in the statutes and ordinances, as brilliantly clear as vermilion. For the past hundred and eighty years, the laws have commanded respect, and people have not dared violate them; money has circulated, and no one has obstructed it. These are what we call sound laws and excellent intentions, enduring, thorough, and meticulous: they ought to be observed in succession for ten thousand generations without ill effect.
Yet what can be done? Laws long in force inevitably reach their limits, and laws that reach their limits must change. To adapt them through change and relieve the straits of all under Heaven, and to determine what is right so that the benefits of all under Heaven are shared equitably—must this not await the Sagely Son of Heaven? Our Emperor models himself on Heaven and treads the path of peace, establishes the supreme standard and enlightens the people, brilliantly perfects rites and music, and refines the governing order. He measures affairs by the Way and maintains the laws, cherishes the penal order and upholds trustworthy standards. The great achievements of his restoration have been gloriously raised up and manifestly established; their brilliance illuminates the universe, without rival. Now that his grand plans and exalted institutions have all borne fruit, the suitability of goods and the needs of the people…

title: 嘉靖三十四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
咸與丕新頃年以来
照臨幽隱洞察時奸知錢貨之行於民者非
復
二祖
列聖之舊而殽雜巧偽之徒私鑄濫惡之物以
阻壞錢法天下之弊極矣乃一旦
渙號布令與民更新特鑄嘉靖通寶悉復
祖宗之制與前代五銖開元之輕重適中者兼
行於天下凡民間殽偽之錢悉罷之行之
===
未幾而市肆不易物貨稱平
朝野之民罔不習而安之喁喁然欣說而謳
吟矣錢之宿蠹朝令而夕除錢之便宜家
喻而戶曉此誠
聖作物覩人心轉移而因革損益燁燁乎宜民
之

革宿弊而利天下之人民者將不豫為
今日揚厲邪夫權操於上則博禍除而七福
